content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a method to measure the misalignment between inverse codes and synthetic distributions. More specifically, it uses cosine distance (SNCD) between style space codes as the metric, and asks the inverse code to be close to the mean of sampled synthetic style space codes.  SNCD is can be added to encoder or optimization based GAN inverse to improve the perception and editablity.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

--Improving GAN inversion is a very fundamental problem, and can have great impact in many image editing/processing applications. So this topic is quite important.

--The analysis of why z, w and s space codes are not unique for inversion is interesting and helpful.

--The proposed method is simple and easy to understand.


Weakness:

--The major technical novelty of this paper is a Cosine distance metric between normalized style space codes, and hence the technical contribution is not high. (Actually, cosine distance for normalized style space codes is the same as Cosine distance for style space codes.)

--The quantitative experiments are only in one domain (face) and evaluation is done with only one data set (CelebA-HQ), make it less convincing.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Overall, the paper is clearly presented and easy to follow. The proposed idea contains some novelty, though the technical contribution is not very high.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this paper is on a very interesting and important topic, with a simple but reasonable solution. I enjoyed reading it. The technical contribution is a little limited, but there are some novelty in the idea. The evaluation can be improved, especially the quantitative evaluations.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper discusses how to acquire better GAN Inversion in terms of fidelity, perception, and editability. While the inversion often goes through two steps, including Image Embedding and Result Refinement, the paper points out that perception and editability mostly come from the first step and are related to the degree of alignment of the inverse codes with the synthetic distribution. Then, it proposes LSAP, a novel inversion paradigm consisting of an evaluation metric and a solution for this problem. LSAP relies on the Normalized Style Space, denoted as S^N, and the cosine distance on this space, denoted as SNCD, to measure the mentioned latent alignment. It then employs SNCD as a loss function to improve inversion results for both encoder-based and optimization-based approaches. LSAP conducts experiments on 4 common datasets to confirm its effectiveness.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
- The paper has an interesting discussion on latent distribution misalignment, how to define a good space, and a metric to measure it. The use of the Normalized Style Space is novel, interesting, and somewhat reasonable.
- The paper conducts a large number of experiments to verify the effectiveness of the proposed approach, using 4 datasets, 6 baselines, and 4 LSAP variants.
- The paper already covers recent techniques like HFGI and SAM.

### Weaknesses
- Corollary 3.1 is only correct in W+ and S space. It is not suitable for W space, in which p_l must be the same in every layer l, and we can not use Property 3.1-3.3 to define p'. It breaks the foundation of the proposed method on W space. Similarly, it is not suitable for Z space.
- While LSAP can align the inverted latents in S_N space, the corresponding w latents may not be aligned. However, common editing operators are learned to execute on W/W+ space. Hence, LSAP may not guarantee good editing results.
- In Section 4.1, the authors assume s^N_{syn} and s^N_{inv} independent. In fact, they are not independent since the inverted latents are learned to approximate the synthetic ones.
- Some experimental results in Table 1, Fig. 3, Fig. 10, and Fig. 11 are missing unreasonably. For example,, while Table 1 has LEC_pose values for encoder-based inversions and fidelity scores for optimization-based inversions, it does not have LEC_pose values for optimization-based inversions. Fig. 3 shows age editing results for encoder-based methods and other editing results for optimization-based inversions, but not the age editing results for optimization-based inversions. It does not make sense since optimization-based inversions are already available, and the learned editing directions should be applicable to both types of inversions. 
- The paper should define or provide a citation for the LEC metric before using it.
- L_{sim} in Equation 12 and Similarity metric in Table 1 & 3 are not defined.
- I would love to see results with one of the generator-finetuned-based methods (PTI/HyperInverter/HyperStyle) and its LSAP counterpart. While HFGI and SAM are quite good and recent, they use a different approach by optimizing the latent vectors/maps.
- In Fig. 4, inverted latents of LSAP_E concentrate in a very small region in S^N space, which is not good. The distribution of e4e latents looks more reasonable.
- Table 2 should be repeated for optimization-based methods.
- Fig. 5 should include the input image. Fig. 6-7 should include the input and the reconstructed images.
- The caption of Table 4: "Quantity" -> "Quantitative"..
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity
- Corollary 3.1 claims to work on Z and W spaces but its formulation seems to be suitable for W+ space. 
- Some experimental results in Table 1, Fig. 3, Fig. 10, and Fig. 11 are missing unreasonably. 
- The paper should define or provide a citation for the LEC metric before using it.
- L_{sim} in Equation 12 and Similarity metric in Table 1 & 3 are not defined.
- Fig. 5 should include the input image. Fig. 6-7 should include the input and the reconstructed images.

### Quality
The paper is interesting and has some merits. However, there are some doubts on its theoretical foundation, as mentioned in the Weaknesses section. The writing needs some improvements as mentioned in the Weakness section.

### Novelty
The proposed method is novel.

### Reproducibility
Code is attached in the supplementary.

The paper has an interesting discussion on latent distribution misalignment, how to define a good space, and a metric to measure it. The use of the Normalized Style Space is novel and interesting. The writing needs some improvements.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a method to improve the fidelity and editability of GAN inversion methods. The authors propose to align two latent spaces, namely the synthetic latent space obtained by random sampling and the embedding latent space obtained by running GAN inversion on real images. The authors propose to perform the alignment in a normalized style space (S^N) and a metric based on the cosine distance in this space, which is arguably better than performing alignment in the W/Z/S space in the original StyleGAN model. The experimental results show that the proposed method performs on par with state-of-the-art methods such as HFGI and SAM.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
** Strength **

The paper presents an interesting approach to improve the quality of GAN inversion. As there exists a trade-off between the reconstruction and manipulation quality, investigations in this direction would be well received by the community. 

The technical discussion is nice to read. The proposed method is sound.

** Weakness ** 

(1) The novelty is somewhat limited. The alignment between the inverted and synthetic latent codes are somewhat straightforward, as the concept that inverted latent codes might stay far from the ordinary latent samples is already mentioned in the previous works. 

(2) The comparison baselines are not the state-of-the-art. 
Please consider adding the following baselines to Table 1 and Figure 3. 

    [a] Roich et al., Pivotal Tuning for Latent-based Editing of Real Images, ACM Transaction on Graphics 2021. 

    [b] Dinh et al., HyperInverter: Improving StyleGAN Inversion via Hypernetwork, CVPR 2022. 

    [c] Alaluf et al., HyperStyle: StyleGAN Inversion with HyperNetworks for Real Image Editing, CVPR 2022.

(3) Another approach to measure the distance is to consider KL-divergence between P_{inv} and P_{syn}. Did the authors consider this option? More discussions would be nice for deeper understanding of the proposed method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The quality of the experiments is one of my concerns. It seems that the experimental results are incomplete.
- Table 1 is partial: some results are unavailable due to time constraints or poor results. I believe such blanks should be filled with results. 
- Similar issues appear in Figure 3. Some images are left blanked. 

There are some missing implementation details. 
- Equation 10: to compute \mu, how many samples $k$ is required? 

The writing is relatively readable. The writing quality can be improved by addressing the following issues: 
- The related work section is too brief. 
- To measure the quality of the inversion, the authors use three terms: fidelity, perception, and editability. 
At first, I am quite confused on the difference between perception and fidelity. Should perception be part of fidelity? Later in the writing it turns out that perception is grouped with editability. I wonder if it is possible to simply say fidelity and editability. I guess the preservation of fidelity, e.g., face identity is implied in editability. 
- There should be a space between the citation and the last character of its preceding word. 
- Table 1: the methods should be annotated or grouped, showing which is encoder-based and which is optimization-based. 
- The equations can be simplified, e.g, equation 3 and 4. Some multiple-line equations should be numbered once, e.g., equation 10 and 11. 
- L_{d-neg} in Equation 12 is not discussed. 
- References to the metric LPIPS and LEC should be added. 
- There are too many references to appendix in the main text.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents an interesting approach to improve the fidelity and editability for GAN inversion, but the experiments are not sufficient to justify its technical contribution. While the concept is clear, the presentation and experiment quality are below the ICLR standard. Therefore, my rating is a clear rejection.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper divides the process of GAN inversion into two steps: 1) Image Embedding and 2) Result Refinement. The paper discusses that most of the existing methods focus only on Step 2, which offers fidelity, and pay little attention to Step 1, which does not improve perception and editability. The authors analyze that perception and editability must be considered during Step 1 and find that this can be done by matching the degree of alignment of the inverse codes with the synthetic distribution. To address this, they propose LSAP and show that the inversion models can benefit from their proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The idea is interesting, but I do not see a big difference in the main results. It needs more rigorous backup experiments, highlighting the difference. In my humble opinion, it is difficult to convince the reader in its current state. In addition, the presentation/writing should be improved. For more details, please see below.

Questions on Property 3.1 and its proof: 
* From what I understand the subscripts at the cases of \hat{s_n} should be l(ell) not n; \hat{s_n} is s_l (when n \neq l) or a \time s_l (when n=l). If not, it is very weird to read. 
* Specify what k means: is a det of S space latent codes for l-th layer \in {1,\cdots, k}.  
* The layer number l is integer, so its range cannot be continuous: [1,k] -> {1, \cdots, k}. 
* In A.1, eq. 16, s^i_l should be squared (as well as in eq. 17)
* If I understood correctly, I think the scale ‘a’ should be restricted to be a positive number by design. When ‘a’<0, property 3.1 does not hold. (the sign of W becomes opposite, and the resulting output may change)

The high-level intuition of the paper is to make the synthetic distribution and the inverse latent distribution match (or align). I agree on this. Here, the alignment is defined in distribution level. However, in the followings, the authors reduce this down to the angle alignment between two latent codes. Isn’t this a too big jump? How can the alignment in angles be considered as a representative feature for the degree of alignment between two distributions? Isn’t this too bold to say so? I understand the logics behind Corollary 3.1, but this needs more discussion or justification. 

“However, perception and editability are inherited from the first step, by inverse codes specifically. In other words, these two properties are not enhanced in this step and are even damaged.” -> Where can I find the reason? I see that Figure 3 gives some qualitative results, but since this is the basis of the main argument, I think this needs more thorough analyses (more experiments and in-depth discussions). For now, it seems like they cannot be strictly disentangled.

Minor
* “there is a lack of limitation of inverse latent space distribution.” -> Cannot understand what this sentence means. Does this mean that since there is no encoder in the optimization methods, it does not have errors that come from the suboptimal encoder? 
* In the encoder method, is it correct to understand that the mapping function I (X->P_inv) is equal to the encoder E?
* In eq. (6), the authors assume that the normalized styles are independent. How? 
* Unlike the description in Appendix E, e4e results looks better. Which point should I focus on? 


Presentation/writings:
* page 2. First bullet point of the key contributions. “…while perception and fidelity are related to alignment between…” -> perception and editability
* page 4. “…a essential problem is obtaining latent codes…” -> an essential problem
* “an intuition idea is that…” ->Noun + Noun, Write either “The intuition is that” or “The idea is that”… (this applies to everywhere else in the main text) 
* Page 7, what is LEC? I guess “latent editing consistency” in e4e, but this is not introduced anywhere in the main text. Every abbreviation in the paper should be introduced with its full name before it is used.  
* Even though the results are unnatural, it looks bad to see the empty spaces in Table 1 and Figure 3, please report all the results.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is okay and has every component to reproduce the work. However, the main argument needs to be supported with more experiments in various perspectives in a more aggressive way.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the idea of the paper is interesting, but further research is needed.

content.title: LSAP: Rethinking Inversion Fidelity, Perception and Editability in GAN Latent Space
content.abstract: As the methods evolve, inversion is mainly divided into two steps. The first step is Image Embedding, in which an encoder or optimization process embeds images to get the corresponding latent codes. Afterward, the second step aims to refine the inversion and editing results, which we named Result Refinement. Although the second step significantly improves fidelity, perception and editability are almost unchanged, deeply dependent on inverse latent codes attained in the first step. Therefore, a crucial problem is gaining the latent codes with better perception and editability while retaining the reconstruction fidelity. In this work, we first point out that these two characteristics are related to the degree of alignment (or disalignment) of the inverse codes with the synthetic distribution. Then, we propose Latent Space Alignment Inversion Paradigm (LSAP), which consists of evaluation metric and solution for this problem. Specifically, we introduce Normalized Style Space ($\mathcal{S^N}$ space) and $\mathcal{S^N}$ Cosine Distance (SNCD) to measure disalignment of inversion methods. Since our proposed SNCD is differentiable, it can be optimized in both encoder-based and optimization-based embedding methods to conduct a uniform solution. Extensive experiments in various domains demonstrate that SNCD effectively reflects perception and editability, and our alignment paradigm archives the state-of-the-art in both two steps.
